SECT 118.185 Partial exemption where dwelling was your main residence during part only of ownership period ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 118.185 **Partial exemption where dwelling was your main residence during part only of ownership period** (1) You get only a [partial](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) exemption for a \\* CGT event that happens in relation to a \\* dwelling or your \\* [ownership interest](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_interest) in it if: (a) you are an [individual](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#individual); and (b) the dwelling was your main residence for [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) only of your \* [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period); and (c) the interest did not \\* pass to you as a beneficiary in, and you did not \\* acquire it as a [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of, the estate of a deceased [person](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#person). (2) You calculate your \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss using the [formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s152.125.html#formula): ![Start formula CG or CL amount times start fraction Non-main residence days over Days in your *ownership period end fraction end formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A05138_image.118.png) where: "CG or CL amount" is the \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss you would have made from the \\* CGT event apart from this Subdivision. "non-main residence days" is the number of days in your \\* [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period) when the \\* dwelling was not your main residence. Note: The capital gain or loss may be further adjusted if the dwelling was used to produce assessable income: see section 118 \- 190\. Example: You bought a house in July 2020 and moved in immediately. In July 2023, you moved out and began to rent it. You sold it in July 2030, making (apart from this Subdivision) a capital gain of $10,000. At the time you sold the house, you were an Australian resident. You choose to continue to treat the dwelling as your main residence [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section 118 \- 145 (about absences) for the first 6 of the 7 years during which you rented the house out. [Under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) this section, you will be taken to have made a capital gain of: ![Start formula $10,000 times start fraction 365 over 3,650 end fraction equals $1,000 end formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A05138_image.119.png) (3) However, this section does not apply if, at the time the \* CGT event happens, you: (a) are an \\* excluded foreign resident; or (b) are a foreign resident who does not satisfy the \* [life events test](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#life_events_test). #### Navigate - SECT 118.192 Special rule for first use to produce income ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 118.192 **Special rule for first use to produce income** (1) There is a special rule if: (a) you would get only a [partial](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) exemption [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) this Subdivision for a \\* CGT event happening in relation to a \\* dwelling or your \* [ownership interest](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_interest) in it because the dwelling was used for the \* [purpose of producing assessable income](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#purpose_of_producing_assessable_income) during your \\* [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period); and (aa) that use occurred for the first time after 7.30 pm, by legal time in the Australian Capital Territory, on 20 August 1996; and (b) you would have got a full exemption [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) this Subdivision if the CGT event had happened just before the first time (the income time ) it was used for that purpose during your [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period). (2) You are taken to have \\* acquired the \\* dwelling or your \* [ownership interest](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_interest) at the income time for its \\* [market value](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#market_value) at that time. (3) If your \\* [ownership interest](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_interest) in the \\* dwelling \\* passed to you as a beneficiary in a deceased estate, or you owned it as the [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of a deceased estate and the \\* CGT event did not happen within 2 years of the deceased's death, you apply this Subdivision as if: (a) you had \\* acquired the interest as an [individual](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#individual) and not as a beneficiary or [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of a deceased estate; and (b) for applying the [formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s164.15.html#formula) in section 118 \- 185, your non \- main residence days were the number of days in your \\* [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period) when the dwelling was not the main residence of an [individual](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#individual) referred to in item 2, column 3 of the table in section 118 \- 195\. Note: There are special rules for dwellings acquired before 7.30 pm on 20 August 1996: see section 118 \- 195 of the [Income Tax (Transitional Provisions) Act 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itpa1997402/). #### Navigate - [Rental property becomes your main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#ato-Rentalpropertybecomesyourmainresidence) ## How it works [Your main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/eligibility-for-main-residence-exemption) (your home) is exempt from capital gains tax (CGT) if you are an Australian resident. You’re not entitled to the full main residence exemption from CGT if you rent out part of your home or run a business from home. However, you may be entitled to a partial main residence exemption. When you sell your home, the part you used to earn assessable income (as a rental or to run a business) is subject to CGT. You can usually claim income tax deductions for the part of your home used to produce assessable income. To work out your capital gain or loss, you consider: - the floor area used as a rental or to run a business, including through the [sharing economy](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/sharing-economy-and-tax/renting-out-all-or-part-of-your-home) - the period you used it for this purpose - if you [first started using your home for rental or business](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Valueofhomewhenfirstusedtoproduceincome) after 20 August 1996. If you're a foreign resident when a [CGT event](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-events) happens to your residential property in Australia (for example, you sell it), generally you aren't entitled to claim the main residence exemption. For more information, see [Main residence exemption for foreign residents](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/foreign-residents-and-capital-gains-tax/main-residence-exemption-for-foreign-residents). ## Check if CGT applies To work out if CGT applies, you need to determine if you would be allowed a deduction for your home loan interest if you had borrowed money to acquire your home. This is the ‘interest deductibility test’. The interest deductibility test must be applied even if you haven't borrowed money to acquire your home. If you are or would be eligible to claim part of the interest expense, your home is subject to CGT to the same extent. If you have a home loan, you can’t: - reduce the capital gain by not claiming a deduction for some or all of the interest - increase the cost base of your home by the amount of interest you choose not to claim as a deduction. You can still get a full main residence exemption if someone else uses part of your home to produce assessable income and you don't receive assessable income from that person for the use of the property. To help work out if you need to consider CGT, check the scenarios in [Capital gains tax and the main residence exemption](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-and-super-professionals/for-tax-professionals/prepare-and-lodge/tax-time/tax-time-toolkits/tax-time-toolkit-for-investors/capital-gains-tax-and-the-main-residence-exemption). ### Renting out part of your home If you rent out part of your home for a period: - You can claim a deduction for the home loan interest related to the portion of your home that is rented out. - The capital gain (or loss) for that portion of your home during the rental period would be assessable – for example, the floor area used by tenants. ### Running a business from home You're running a business from home if it’s your principal place of business and you have space set aside just for this purpose. Merely working from home occasionally or by choice doesn’t qualify. You're only eligible for the full main residence exemption if you’re not entitled to claim a deduction for interest expenses. You’re entitled to claim a deduction for part of any home loan interest if: - part of your home is set aside exclusively as a place of business and is clearly identifiable as such - that part of the home isn’t readily adaptable for private use – for example, a doctor's surgery located in a doctor's home. You’re **not** entitled to claim a deduction for interest expenses if you: - use a home study to do work usually done at your place of work - do paid child-minding at home (unless part of your home is set aside exclusively for that purpose). If you’re not entitled to a full main residence exemption because you use your home for business purposes, you may be able to apply the [small business CGT concessions](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/incentives-and-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions) to reduce your capital gain. ## Work out your capital gain or loss You can use the [CGT property exemption tool](https://www.ato.gov.au/calculators-and-tools/capital-gains-tax-property-exemption-tool) to calculate the portion of your home that is subject to CGT. Alternatively, you can work out the assessable part of your capital gain or loss as follows: **Step 1:** Work out the capital gain or loss on your home based on its value when you first used it to produce assessable income. There are exceptions if you first used your home to produce assessable income before 21 August 1996 or inherited your home. For more information see [Value of home when first used to produce income](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Valueofhomewhenfirstusedtoproduceincome). **Step 2:** Determine the portion of your home's floor area that you set aside to produce assessable income. **Step 3:** Multiply steps 1 and 2. If you: - used your home to produce assessable income right up to when you sold it, this is your assessable capital gain or loss – you don’t need to continue - stopped using your home to produce assessable income before you sold it – continue to step 4. **Step 4:** Determine the number of days you used your home to produce assessable income. **Step 5:** Determine the number of days from the date you first used your home to produce assessable income until you sold it. **Step 6:** Your net capital gain is step 3 × (step 4 ÷ step 5). ### Example: part of home rented throughout ownership period Thomas bought a house on 1 July 2003 for $300,000. He sold it on 30 June 2026 for $700,000. The house was his main residence for the entire time. Throughout the period Thomas owned the house a tenant rented one bedroom, which represented 20% of the house. Both Thomas and the tenant used the living room, bathroom, laundry and kitchen, which represented 30% of the house. Only Thomas used the remainder of the house. This means Thomas is entitled to a 35% deduction (20% + \[30% × 50%\]) for home loan interest (if he incurred it). Using [steps 1 to 6](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Workouttheassessablepartofyourcapitalgai) Thomas works out his net capital gain as follows. 1. Thomas used his home to produce assessable income from the time he acquired it. Therefore, he uses its initial value to work out his capital gain: $700,000 − $300,000 = $400,000. 2. The portion of the floor area set aside for rental is 35%. 3. Thomas' net capital gain is $400,000 × 35% = $140,000. As he used his home to earn assessable income right up to when he sold it, he doesn’t need to apportion his net capital gain for any period it wasn’t used to produce assessable income. As Thomas owned his house for at least 12 months he can use the CGT discount (50% for individuals) to reduce his capital gain. Thomas's net capital gain would be $70,000. End of example ### Example: part of home used for business for part of ownership period Fatima bought a house in December 1997 for $200,000. It was her main residence. - On 1 November 2018 she started to use 40% of the house for a consultancy business. At that time the market value of the house was $520,000. - On 1 August 2022 she shifted her consultancy practice to separate business premises and used her home solely for private purposes. - On 1 May 2026 she sold her house for $620,000. Using the [steps 1 to 6](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Workouttheassessablepartofyourcapitalgai), Fatima works out her net capital gain as follows: 1. Her capital gain based on the value of her home when she first used it to produce assessable income is $620,000 − $520,000 = $100,000. 2. The portion of her home's floor area set aside for business was 40%. 3. $100,000 × 40% = $40,000. As Fatima stopped using her home for business before she sold it, she continues to step 4. 4. Fatima used her home to produce assessable income from 1 November 2018 to 1 August 2022, a total of 1,370 days. 5. The period from when she first used her home to produce assessable income until she sold it is 2,739 days (1 November 2018 to 1 May 2026). 6. Fatima's net capital gain is $40,000 × (1,370 ÷ 2,739) = $20,007. For CGT purposes, Fatima is treated as if she acquired the house on 1 November 2018. This is more than 12 months before she sold it, so she can use the CGT discount (50% for individuals) to reduce her capital gain. Fatima's net capital gain would be $10,003. End of example ## Value of home when first used to produce income If you use your home to produce assessable income you are generally taken to have acquired it at the time you first used it for this purpose. This means when you sell your home, you need to use the 'home first used to produce income rule'. You do this by working out the capital gain or loss using its market value at the time you first used it to produce assessable income. If you sell your home within 12 months of when you first use it to produce assessable income, you can’t use the [CGT discount](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-12monthownershiprequirement). ### Market valuation You must get a [market valuation](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/market-valuation-of-assets) of your home when you first start using it for rental or business, if this was after 20 August 1996. You need to know this value to calculate your capital gain or loss when you sell it. ### Exclusions to the 'home first used to produce income rule' The 'home first used to produce income rule' doesn't apply if you: - use your home to produce assessable income from the time you acquire it, the rule doesn’t affect you – for an example, see [Rental property becomes your main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Rentalpropertybecomesyourmainreside) - [inherit a dwelling](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/inherited-assets-and-capital-gains-tax/inherited-property-and-cgt) that was a deceased’s main residence – the rule doesn’t apply when you sell the dwelling within 2 years - choose to [continue treating a property as your main residence after you move out](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/treating-former-home-as-main-residence) – when the property is fully exempt, the rule doesn’t apply - don't meet the criteria for a partial main residence exemption, – for example, you either - were a foreign resident when you sold the property - claimed the exemption for another property for the period you lived there. #### Example: 'home first used to produce income rule' doesn't apply Peter bought a house on 1 October 2013 for $550,000. He rented it out until 30 June 2016. Peter moved into the house on 1 July 2016 and lived in it for the entire period until it was sold on 30 March 2026 for $780,000. The ‘home first used to produce income rule’ doesn’t apply as the house was rented from the time Peter bought it. This means that Peter isn’t required to use the market value of the house at the time it was first used to produce assessable income. Peter works out the capital gain based on the cost base of $550,000. Peter is entitled to the main residence exemption from 1 July 2016 to 30 March 2026 (3,560 days). The assessable part of Peter’s capital gain will be calculated as follows: 1. Capital gain for the entire period is $780,000 − $550,000 = $230,000 2. Peter’s home was rented out for 1,004 days (1 October 2013 to 30 June 2016) 3. Peter’s total period of ownership was 4,564 days. 4. Capital gain for the period that was rented out is $230,000 × (1,004 ÷ 4,564) = $50,595. Peter is entitled to the CGT discount of 50% which will reduce his capital gain. Peter’s net capital gain would be $25,297. End of example ### When the rule applies Apart from these exclusions, the rule applies if all the following are true: - you acquired the property on or after 20 September 1985 - you first used the property to produce assessable income after 20 August 1996 - when you sell the property (or another [CGT event](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-events) happens to it), you would be entitled to a partial CGT exemption because you used it to produce assessable income during the time you owned it - you would have been entitled to a full exemption if the sale or other CGT event happened to the property immediately before you first used it to produce assessable income. #### Example: home becomes a rental property Erin bought a house 25 July 2014 for $450,000. The house was her main residence until she moved into a new house on 1 August 2025. On 2 August 2025 she began renting out the old house. At that time, the market value of the old house was $650,000. Erin didn’t want to treat the old house as her main residence under the ‘continuing main residence status after moving out’ option. She wanted the new house to be treated as her main residence from the date she moved into it. On 10 June 2026 Erin sold the old house for $696,000. As Erin is deemed to have acquired the old house for $650,000 on 2 August 2025, she calculates her capital gain to be $46,000. She can’t use the CGT discount to reduce her capital gain as she is taken to have owned it for less than 12 months. For the period the property was rented out, you will be liable for CGT when you sell the property. Use the following formula to work out your CGT when you sell your property: Capital gain or loss × (number of days the property was used to produce assessable income ÷ total number of days you owned the property) The total number of days you owned the property is calculated using the contract purchase and sale dates, not settlement dates. You can also use the [Capital gains tax property exemption tool](https://www.ato.gov.au/calculators-and-tools/capital-gains-tax-property-exemption-tool) to work out what percentage of your capital gain is exempt from CGT. ### Example: rental property becomes your home Farnaz entered into a contract to purchase a property on 21 October 2019 for $449,000. She immediately rented out the property. The property was rented for 2 years, until Farnaz moved into the property on 16 November 2021. Farnaz lived in the property as her main residence until she signed a contract to sell her home on 1 April 2026 for $987,500. Farnaz works out her net capital gain as follows: 1. Capital gain is $538,500 (worked out as $987,500 − $449,000) 2. Number of days owned is 2,355 (21 October 2019 to 1 April 2026) 3. Number of days the property was used to produce assessable income is 757 (21 October 2019 to 15 November 2021) 4. Assessable capital gain is $538,500 × (757 ÷ 2,355) = $173,097 5. Net capital gain after applying the 50% CGT discount for owning the property for over 12 months is $86,548 (worked out as $173,097 × 50%) Farnaz includes a net capital gain of $86,548 in her 2026 tax return. Note 1: You need to keep records of [each](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#each) element: see Division 121\. Note 2: The cost base is reduced by [net input tax credits](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_input_tax_credit): see section 103 \- 30\. Note 3: An amount that [makes](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) up all or [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) of an element of the cost base of an asset may be determined [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section [230](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s230.html)\- [505](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s505.html), if the amount is [provided](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#provide) for acquiring a thing, and you start or cease to have a Division 230 financial arrangement as consideration for the acquisition of the thing. 5 elements of the cost base (2) The first element is the total of: (a) the [money](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#money) you paid, or are required to pay, in respect of \* acquiring it; and (b) the \\* [market value](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#market_value) of any other property you gave, or are required to give, in respect of acquiring it (worked out as at the time of the acquisition). Note 1: There are [special](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#special) rules for working out when you are required to pay [money](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#money) or give other property: see section 103 \- 15\. Note 2: This element is replaced with another amount in many situations: see Division 112\. These costs can include giving property: see section 103 \- 5\. Note: There is one situation to do with options in [which](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#which) the [incidental costs](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#incidental_costs) relating to the CGT event are modified: see section 112 \- [85](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s85.html). (4) The third element is the costs of owning the \\* CGT asset you incurred (but only if you \\* acquired the asset after 20 August 1991). These costs include: (a) interest on [money](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#money) you borrowed to acquire the asset; and (b) costs of maintaining, repairing or insuring it; and (c) rates or land tax, if the asset is land; and (d) interest on [money](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#money) you borrowed to refinance the [money](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#money) you borrowed to acquire the asset; and (e) interest on [money](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#money) you borrowed to finance the capital expenditure you incurred to increase the asset's [value](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#value). These costs can include giving property: see section 103 \- 5\. Note: This element does not apply to [personal use assets](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#personal_use_asset) or collectables: see sections 108 \- [17](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s17.html) and 108 \- 30\. (5) The fourth element is capital expenditure you incurred: (a) the purpose or the expected effect of [which](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#which) is to increase or preserve the asset's [value](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#value); or (b) that relates to installing or moving the asset. (6) The fifth element is capital expenditure that you incurred to establish, preserve or defend your title to the asset, or a right [over](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#over) the asset. Assume a CGT event for purposes of working out cost base at a [particular](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) time (12) If: (a) it is necessary to work out the \\* cost base at a [particular](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) time; and (b) a \\* CGT event does not happen in relation to the asset at or just after that time; assume, for the purpose only of working out the cost base at the [particular](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) time, that such an event does happen in relation to the asset at or just after that time. Note 1: For example, in order to apply [subsection](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.40.html#subsection)110 \- 37(1), it is necessary for there to be a CGT event. Note 2: The assumption that a CGT event happens does not have any consequence beyond that stated. For example, it does not mean that the asset is afterwards to be treated as having been acquired at the [particular](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) time with a first element of cost base equal to all of its former cost base elements. #### Navigate - (The expenditure mentioned in this section can include giving property: see section 103 \- 5.) For the cost base of interests in [partnership](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#partnership) assets acquired after that time, see section 110 \- 50\. For exceptions to the application of this section, see section 110 - 53\. (1A) This section also applies to expenditure incurred after 30 June 1999 on land or a building if: (a) the land or building was \\* acquired at or before the time mentioned in [subsection](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s110.50.html#subsection)(1); and (b) the expenditure forms [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) of the fourth element of the \* cost base of the land or building. Deductible expenditure excluded from second and third elements (1B) Expenditure does not form [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) of the second or third element of the cost base to the extent that you have deducted or can deduct it. Other deductible expenditure (2) Expenditure (except expenditure excluded by [subsection](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s110.50.html#subsection)(1B)) does not form [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) of the cost base to the extent that you have deducted or can deduct it for an [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year), except so far as: (a) the [deduction](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#deduction) has been reversed by an amount being included in your assessable income for an [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) by a provision of [this Act](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#this_act) (outside this [Part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) and [Part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part)3 \- 3 and Division 243); or Note: Division 20 contains some of the provisions that reverse [deductions](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#deduction). Section 20 \- 5 lists some others. (ab) the [deduction](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#deduction) is [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) Division 243; or (b) the [deduction](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#deduction) would have been so reversed apart from a provision listed in the table (relief from including a balancing charge in your assessable income). | Provisions for relief from including a balancing charge in your<br>assessable income | | --- | | Item | Provision | Subject matter | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | section 40 \- 340 | Roll<br>\- [over](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#over) relief for \\* depreciating asset | | 2 | section 40 \- 365 | Involuntary<br>disposal of \\* depreciating asset | Recouped expenditure (3) Expenditure does not form [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) of any element of the cost base to the extent of any amount you have received as \\* [recoupment](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#recoupment) of it, except so far as the amount is included in your assessable income. Landcare and [water facility](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#water_facility) expenditure giving rise to a [tax offset](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#tax_offset) (5) Expenditure does not form [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) of the cost base to the extent that you choose a \\* [tax offset](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#tax_offset) for it [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) the former section 388 \- [55](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s55.html) (about the landcare and [water facility](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#water_facility) [tax offset](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#tax_offset)) instead of deducting it. correctness.justification: Correct rules and sections throughout: s 118-192 resets the first element to $420,000 market value, pre-2020 costs dropped, $30,000 renovation (s 110-25(5)) and $20,000 agent fees (s 110-25(3)) added to give $470,000, gain of $530,000, then s 118-185 pro-rata from the deemed acquisition date. The 366/1096 day count (correctly reflecting the 2020 leap year) yields $176,989 versus the reference's 365/1097 and $176,345 — a defensible, arguably more precise convention, transparently flagged — and the headline frames $530,000 as 'the capital gain' where s 118-185(2) technically makes the pro-rated figure the capital gain, a small terminological slip; operative words are not quoted verbatim, which level 5 requires.

completeness.justification: Covers every key limb of the reference: s 118-192 reset and its conditions, disregard of the $300,000 price and $10,000 stamp duty, both cost-base additions with correct elements, the $530,000 gain, the deemed-acquisition start date for the ownership period, and the day-count pro-rata — plus extras (unavailability of the 6-year rule, s 110-45/Div 43 caveat, discount eligibility). The only notable omission is naming CGT event A1 (s 104-10), a minor point.

faithfulness.justification: Around 90%+ of load-bearing claims are anchored at the claim and verified by captured text (6-year-rule exclusivity via [1], s 118-185 formula via [2], s 118-192 conditions and deemed acquisition via [3] and [4], cost-base elements via [5], s 110-45 via [6]). Only minor items float free — the 50%-discount eligibility sentence and the 'three figures are irrelevant' inference (though the latter follows from verified premises) — and the answer paraphrases rather than sets out the operative statutory words verbatim, which bars a 5.

helpfulness.justification: Well-structured with a workings table, explicit day-count computation, sensitivity note on counting conventions, and a professionally relevant Div 43 caveat flagging the action needed (verify rate/eligibility). It lacks a verbatim set-out of the governing words and an explicit 'read next' pointer, so it sits at level 4 rather than 5.

citation_grounding.justification: Every material claim is anchored at the claim to authority whose captured text verifies it: the full texts of ss 118-185, 118-192, 110-25 and 110-45 are captured (including the s 118-185 formula and s 118-192(2) deemed-acquisition words), and the ATO pages are used only for practice points whose captured passages genuinely support them (the 'can't treat any other property' passage, the Roya example's day count 'from deemed acquisition date', and the Erin example on all fours). Dense, multi-source, primary-first grounding with no irrelevant or unsupportive citations.

judge_output.summary: Correct methodology and figures (s 118-192 reset to $420,000, $470,000 cost base, $530,000 gain, ~$177k after s 118-185 pro-rata), densely anchored to captured primary legislation; minor day-count convention difference and paraphrase-rather-than-quotation keep it short of full marks on some dimensions.

[Follow @AustLII on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/user?screen_name=AustLII) [[2]] CGT discount | Australian Taxation Office — https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount extract (page read): [Skip to main content](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#content) [Skip To search](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#search-box) [Skip To Alex Virtual Assistant](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#alex-virtual-assistant) # CGT discount Find out if your asset is eligible for the 50% CGT discount. **Last updated** 29 June 2026 Print or Download Info Alert Recent capital gains tax changes Recent changes to capital gains tax (CGT) announced in the 2026–27 Federal Budget don’t apply to Tax Time 2026. ## On this page - [How the CGT discount works](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-HowtheCGTdiscountworks) - [12-month ownership requirement](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-12monthownershiprequirement) - [Exclusions from the CGT discount](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-ExclusionsfromtheCGTdiscount) - [Trusts and companies](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-Trustsandcompanies) - [How to use the CGT discount](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-HowtousetheCGTdiscount) - [Extra discount for affordable rental housing](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-Extradiscountforaffordablerentalhousing) ## How the CGT discount works When you sell or otherwise dispose of an asset, you can reduce your capital gain by 50%, if both of the following apply: - you owned the asset for at least 12 months - you are an Australian resident for tax purposes. This is called the capital gains tax (CGT) discount. ## 12-month ownership requirement For an asset to qualify for the CGT discount you must own it for at least 12 months before the 'CGT event' happens. The CGT event is the point at which you make a capital gain or loss. You exclude the day of acquisition and the day of the CGT event when working out if you owned the CGT asset for at least 12 months before the 'CGT event’ happens. - **If you sell the asset and there is no contract of sale**, the CGT event happens at the time of sale. - **If there is a contract to sell the asset**, the CGT event happens on the date of the contract, not when you settle. Property sales usually work this way. - **If the asset is lost or destroyed**, the CGT event happens when: - you first receive an insurance payment or other compensation - if there is no insurance payment or compensation, when the loss occurred or was discovered. You can count an asset’s previous ownership towards your 12-month ownership period if you acquired it: - through a [deceased estate](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/inherited-assets-and-capital-gains-tax/inherited-property-and-cgt) if the asset was acquired by the deceased on or after 20 September 1985 - through a [relationship breakdown](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/relationship-breakdown-and-capital-gains-tax/main-residence-exemption-in-relationship-breakdown) – you will satisfy the 12–month requirement if the combined period your spouse and you owned the asset was more than 12 months - as a rollover replacement for an asset that was lost, destroyed or compulsorily acquired if the period of ownership of the original asset and the replacement asset was at least 12 months. ## Exclusions from the CGT discount You can't use the CGT discount in the following circumstances. ### Home first used for rental or business in last 12 months If the asset is your home and you first started [using it for rental or business](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business) less than 12 months before disposing of it, you can't use the CGT discount. ### You use the indexation method instead If you have owned the asset since before 21 September 1999, you can [index the cost of the asset for inflation](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/indexing-the-cost-base) instead of using the CGT discount. But in most cases, you will get a better result (a smaller capital gain) by using the discount. ### Foreign or temporary residents The full CGT discount can't be used for capital gains made by [foreign or temporary residents](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/foreign-residents-and-capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount-for-foreign-residents) after 8 May 2012. However, you may get an apportioned discount on capital gains if you had a period of Australian residency during your ownership of the asset. ### Creation of new asset The CGT discount isn't available for a CGT event that creates a new asset and a capital gain. This might happen, for example, with a restrictive covenant, where you receive payment for agreeing not to do something or granting a lease. In these cases the asset hasn't been acquired at least 12 months before the CGT event. ### Disposal of interest in a non-widely held entity The CGT discount may be denied when you dispose of certain shares or trust interests in non-widely held companies and trusts. These are companies and trusts with fewer than 300 members. ### Conversion of income asset If an income asset is converted into a capital asset for the purposes of claiming the CGT discount, the discount may be denied (under Part IVA of the _Income Tax Assessment Act 1936_). ## Trusts and companies If an asset is owned for at least 12 months: - Australian trusts can discount a capital gain by 50% - complying super funds can discount a capital gain by 33.33%. Companies can't use the CGT discount. ## How to use the CGT discount [Calculating your CGT](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt) explains how to use the CGT discount to reduce your tax. Briefly, this is how it works: 1. If you have any capital losses from other assets, you must subtract these from your capital gains before applying the discount. 2. If you are entitled to the discount for an asset, you reduce the remaining capital gain on that asset by 50% and report this amount in your income tax return. Complying super funds reduce their capital gain by 33.33%. ## Extra discount for affordable rental housing There is an additional CGT discount of up to 10% for individuals who are Australian residents for tax purposes who provide [affordable rental housing](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount-for-affordable-housing) to people earning low to moderate income. This increases the CGT discount to up to 60% for owners of these residential rental properties. Step 5. Reduce by the \\* discount percentage [each](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#each) amount of any \\* discount capital gain remaining after the application of steps 1 to 4. Note: Only some entities can have discount capital gains, and only if they have capital gains from certain CGT assets acquired at least a year before making the gains: see Division 115\. Step 6. If any of your \\* capital gains (whether or not they are \\* discount capital gains) remaining after step 5 qualify for any of the small [business](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#business) concessions in Subdivisions 152 \- C, 152 \- D and 152 \- E, apply those concessions to [each](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#each) of those capital gains as [provided](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#provide) for in those Subdivisions. Note 1: The basic conditions for getting these concessions are in Subdivision 152 \- A. Note 2: Subdivision 152 \- C does not apply to CGT events J2, J5 and J6. In addition, Subdivision 152 \- E does not apply to CGT events J5 and J6. Step 7. Add up the amounts of any \\* capital gains remaining after step 6. The sum is your [net capital gain](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain)for the [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year). Note: For exceptions and modifications to these rules: see section 102 \- 30\. (2) However, if during the [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year): (a) you became bankrupt; or (b) you were released from debts [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) a law relating to bankruptcy; any \\* [net capital loss](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_loss) you made for an earlier [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) [must](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#must) be disregarded in working out whether you made a \\* [net capital gain](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain) for the [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) or a later one. [Follow @AustLII on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/user?screen_name=AustLII) [[4]] Using capital losses to reduce capital gains | Australian Taxation Office — https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains extract (page read): [Skip to main content](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#content) [Skip To search](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#search-box) [Skip To Alex Virtual Assistant](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#alex-virtual-assistant) # Using capital losses to reduce capital gains Find out when you can use capital losses to reduce your capital gains, and how to carry forward a net capital loss. **Last updated** 22 June 2026 Print or Download ## On this page - [When to use capital losses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Whentousecapitallosses) - [Carrying forward a net capital loss](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Carryingforwardanetcapitalloss) - [Non-allowable capital losses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Nonallowablecapitallosses) - [Capital losses from collectables](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Capitallossesfromcollectables) - [Company capital losses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Companycapitallosses) - [Trust capital losses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Trustcapitallosses) - [Exempt entity losses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#ato-Exemptentitylosses) ## When to use capital losses You use your current year capital losses to offset your current year capital gains. You can choose which capital gains to subtract your capital losses from. If you have any capital gains that are not eligible for the CGT discount, subtract your capital losses from these gains first. This will result in the lowest payable CGT. If you have capital losses from prior years, also known as net capital losses carried forward, you can use them to offset your current year capital gains. If your prior year capital losses extinguished your current year capital gain, you don't have a current year capital gain. As net capital losses can be carried forward indefinitely, there is an order of using your capital losses to offset capital gains. You apply your net capital losses in the order that you make them. There are capital losses you can't use to offset capital gains, they are listed at [non-allowable capital losses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/using-capital-losses-to-reduce-capital-gains#Nonallowablecapitallosses). ## Carrying forward a net capital loss If your allowable capital losses are greater than your capital gains, you have a net capital loss. You can carry it forward to later income years to be deducted from future capital gains. You can’t deduct capital losses or a net capital loss from your other assessable income. There is no time limit on how long you can carry forward a net capital loss. ## Non-allowable capital losses You can't deduct capital losses you make from: - [personal use assets](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/list-of-cgt-assets-and-exemptions#ato-Personaluseassets), for example boats or furniture - assets that are [exempt from CGT](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/list-of-cgt-assets-and-exemptions), for example cars and motorcycles - [collectables below a certain value](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/list-of-cgt-assets-and-exemptions#ato-Collectables) - a lease (whether the result of expiry, forfeiture, surrender or assignment) – except if its main purpose is producing income, for example a commercial rental property or a car - paying [personal services income](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/personal-services-income) to yourself through an entity you have set up _._ ## Capital losses from collectables Capital losses from [collectables](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/list-of-cgt-assets-and-exemptions#ato-Collectables) can only be deducted from capital gains made from collectables. They can't be deducted from gains made from other assets. If you don't have a capital gain from another collectable, you can carry forward the capital loss to deduct it against a gain from a collectable in a future year. A collectable isn't subject to CGT if you acquired it for $500 or less (or acquired an interest in it when it had a market value of $500 or less). This means you ignore a capital gain or loss from the collectable. ## Company capital losses A company can deduct previous net capital losses from capital gains in the current year as long as it is either: - substantially under the same ownership and control - still in the same line of business. ## Trust capital losses Capital losses made by a trust can't be distributed to the trust’s beneficiaries. The trust can carry forward its net capital losses and deduct them from capital gains in future years. ## Exempt entity losses Losses made by an entity that is exempt from income tax are disregarded. For more information and help on how to calculate your CGT, see [Calculating your CGT](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt). SECT 102AG **Trust income to which Division applies** (1) Where a beneficiary of a trust estate is a prescribed [person](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s202a.html#person) in relation to a [year of income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#year_of_income), this Division applies to so much of the [share](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#share) of the beneficiary of the [net income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s102m.html#net_income) of the trust estate of the [year of income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#year_of_income) as, in the opinion of the [Commissioner](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#commissioner), is attributable to [assessable income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#assessable_income) of the trust estate that is not, in relation to that beneficiary, excepted trust [income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s128a.html#income). (2) Subject to this section, an amount included in the [assessable income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#assessable_income) of a trust estate is excepted trust [income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s128a.html#income) in relation to a beneficiary of the trust estate to the extent to which the amount: (a) is [assessable income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#assessable_income), of a kind covered by [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s121l.html#subsection)(2AA), of a trust estate that resulted from: (i) a will, codicil or an order of a court that varied or modified the provisions of a will or codicil; or (ii) an intestacy or an order of a court that varied or modified the application, in relation to the estate of a deceased [person](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s202a.html#person), of the provisions of the law relating to the [distribution](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#distribution) of the estates of [persons](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s202a.html#person) who die intestate; (b) is employment [income](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s128a.html#income); (c) is derived by the [trustee](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#trustee) of the trust estate from the investment of any [property](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s121f.html#property) [transferred](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s343.html#transfer) to the [trustee](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#trustee) for the benefit of the beneficiary: (i) by way of, or in satisfaction of a claim for, damages in respect of: (A) loss by the beneficiary of [parental](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s6.html#parent) support; or (B) [personal](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s202a.html#person) injury to the beneficiary, any disease suffered by the beneficiary or any impairment of the beneficiary's physical or mental condition; (ii) pursuant to any law relating to worker's compensation; (iii) pursuant to any law relating to the payment of compensation in respect of criminal injuries; (iv) directly as the result of the death of a [person](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s202a.html#person) and under the terms of a policy of life insurance; (v) directly as the result of the death of a [person](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s202a.html#person) and out of a [provident](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s21a.html#provide), benefit, superannuation or retirement fund;     extract (page read): ## [![](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/images/tiny-austlii.gif)](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/) Commonwealth Consolidated Acts \[ [Index](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/)\] \[ [Table](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/index.html#s13)\] \[ [Search](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinoform.pl)\] \[ [Search this Act](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinoform.pl/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/)\] \[ [Notes](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/notes.html)\] \[ [Noteup](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinosrch.pl?query=cth+consol_act+itra1986174+s13)\] \[ [Previous](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s12a.html)\] \[ [Next](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s14.html)\] \[ [Download](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/download.cgi/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174)\] \[ [Help](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/help/legis-help.html)\] * * * ### INCOME TAX RATES ACT 1986 - SECT 13 **Rates of tax where Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies** (1) The rates of tax in respect of the taxable income of a resident taxpayer: (a) who is a prescribed person in relation to the year of income for the purposes of Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act; and (b) who has, for the purposes of that Division, an eligible taxable income of an amount exceeding $416; are as set out in Part I of Schedule 11\. (2) Where the eligible taxable income of a resident taxpayer for the purposes of Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act exceeds $416 but does not exceed the resident phase \- out limit, the amount of tax payable under [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(1) in respect of that eligible taxable income shall not exceed: (a) 66% of the amount by which that eligible taxable income exceeds $416; or (b) the amount ascertained by deducting from the amount of tax that would be payable by the taxpayer if the rates set out in Part I of Schedule 7 were applied to the taxable income of the taxpayer the amount of tax that would be payable by the taxpayer if those rates were applied to the taxable income of the taxpayer reduced by the amount of that eligible taxable income; whichever is the greater. (3) Where: (a) a trustee of a trust estate is liable to be assessed and to pay tax under section 98 of the Assessment Act in respect of the share of a resident [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the trust estate; (b) Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies to a part of that share; and (c) the part of that share to which that Division applies exceeds $416; the rates of tax payable by the trustee in respect of that share of the net income of the trust estate are as set out in Part I of Schedule 12\. (4) Where: (a) a trustee of a trust estate is liable to be assessed and to pay tax under section 98 of the Assessment Act in respect of the share of a resident [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the trust estate; (b) Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies to a part of that share; (c) the part of that share to which that Division applies does not exceed $416; (d) Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act also applies to a part of the share of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of another trust estate or to parts of the shares of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net incomes of other trust estates; and (e) the sum of the part referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(b) and the part or parts referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(d) exceeds $416; the trustee of the trust estate referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(a) is liable to pay tax in respect of the share of the net income of the trust estate referred to in that [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph) at the rates set out in Part I of Schedule 12\. (5) Where: (a) the amount of tax that a trustee of a trust estate is liable to pay in respect of the share of a resident [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the trust estate is, by virtue of [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(4), to be calculated in accordance with Part I of Schedule 12; and (b) the sum of: (i) the part of that share to which Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies; and (ii) the part of the share of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the other trust estate or the parts of the shares of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net incomes of the other trust estates, as the case may be, to which that Division applies; does not exceed the resident phase \- out limit; the tax that, apart from this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection), would be payable by the trustee in respect of the share referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(a) shall be reduced by such amount (if any) as, in the opinion of the Commissioner, is fair and reasonable. (6) Subject to [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(7), where: (a) the trustee of a trust estate is liable to be assessed and to pay tax under section 98 of the Assessment Act in respect of the share of a resident [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the trust estate; (b) Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies to a part (in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection) referred to as the eligible part ) of that share; and (c) the eligible part of that share exceeds $416 but does not exceed the resident phase \- out limit; the amount of tax payable under [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(3) in respect of the eligible part of that share shall not exceed: (d) 66% of the amount by which the eligible part of that share exceeds $416; or (e) the amount ascertained by deducting from the amount of tax that would be payable by the trustee if the rates referred to in Part I of Schedule 10 were applied to that share of that net income the amount of tax that would be payable by the trustee if those rates were applied to that share of that net income reduced by the amount of the eligible part of that share; whichever is the greater. (7) [Subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(6) does not apply in relation to the share of a [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of a trust estate if Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies to a part of a share of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of another trust estate or to parts of the shares of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net incomes of other trust estates. (8) Where: (a) by reason of the application of [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(7), [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(6) does not apply in relation to the share of a [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of a trust estate in respect of which a trustee is liable to be assessed and to pay tax under section 98 of the Assessment Act; and (b) the sum of: (i) the part of that share to which Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applies; and (ii) the part of the share of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the other trust estate or the parts of the shares of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net incomes of the other trust estates, as the case may be, to which that Division applies; does not exceed the resident phase \- out limit; the tax that, apart from this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection), would be payable by the trustee in respect of the share referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(a) shall be reduced by such amount (if any) as, in the opinion of the Commissioner, is fair and reasonable. (9) In forming an opinion for the purposes of [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(5) or (8) (in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection) referred to as the relevant [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)) in relation to the share of a [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of a trust estate of a year of income, the Commissioner shall have regard to: (a) any limitation that would be applicable under [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(6) on the amount of tax that would be payable by a trustee in accordance with Part I of Schedule 12 in respect of a share of the net income of a trust estate of the year of income of an amount equal to the sum of the shares referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(b) of the relevant [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection) if: (i) Division 6AA of Part III of the Assessment Act applied to so much of that share as is equal to the sum of the parts of the shares referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s29.html#paragraph)(b) of the relevant [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection); and (ii) that share were a share of a resident [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) who is not presently entitled to a share of the income of the year of income of any other trust estate; (b) the amount of any reduction previously granted by the Commissioner under [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s30.html#subsection)(5) or (8) in relation to the share of the [beneficiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itra1986174/s16.html#beneficiary) of the net income of the year of income of any other trust estate; and (c) such other matters (if any) as the Commissioner thinks fit. [[4]] Tax rates if you're under 18 years old | Australian Taxation Office — https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old
    extract (page read): [Skip to main content](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#content) [Skip To search](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#search-box) [Skip To Alex Virtual Assistant](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#alex-virtual-assistant) # Tax rates if you're under 18 years old Tax payable on income you receive, if you're under 18 years old and not an excepted person with excepted income. **Last updated** 1 June 2026 Print or Download ## On this page - [How tax applies if you're under 18 years old](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#ato-Howtaxappliesifyoureunder18yearsold) - [If you are a resident](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#ato-Ifyouarearesident) - [If you are a non-resident](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#ato-Ifyouareanonresident) - [How income is taxed if you are under 18](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#ato-Howincomeistaxedifyouareunder18) ## How tax applies if you're under 18 years old Special rules apply and you pay tax on certain income types at a higher rate on income you receive if you're under 18 years old. This rule was introduced to discourage adults from diverting income to their children. If you aren't an [excepted person](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/income-you-must-declare/your-income-if-you-are-under-18-years-old#Workoutifyouareanexceptedperson) or receiving [excepted income](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/income-you-must-declare/your-income-if-you-are-under-18-years-old#Exceptedincome), you pay tax on that income as below depending on your residency. You pay the same [individual income tax rates](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-australian-residents) as an adult if you're an excepted person or on excepted income. ## If you are a resident | Income for the year | Tax rates | | --- | --- | | $0 – $416 | Nil | | $417 – $1,307 | Nil plus 66% of the excess over $416 (see [Note](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#Ifyouareanonresident)) | | Over $1,307 | 45% of the total amount of the income that is not excepted income | Table 1: Tax rates for residents who are under 18 for 2025–26 | Income for the year | Tax rates | | --- | --- | | $0 – $416 | Nil | | $417 – $1,307 | Nil plus 66%of the excess over $416 (see [Note](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-if-you-re-under-18-years-old#Ifyouareanonresident)) | | Over $1,307 | 45% of the total amount of the income that is not excepted income | Table 2: Tax rates for residents who are under 18 for 2020–21 to 2024–25 **Note**: This rate, or if it is greater, the rate payable on eligible taxable income if it were the top slice of total taxable income and the general rates applied. ## How income is taxed if you are under 18 | If you... | Then... | | --- | --- | | Are an excepted person | your net income is taxed at the same individual income tax rates as an adult | | Only have excepted income, such as part-time employment income | your excepted net income is taxed at the same individual income tax rates as an adult | | Have some excepted income (such as part-time employment income) and some other income (such as a family trust distribution) | - your excepted net income is taxed at the same individual income tax rates as an adult<br>- your other income (after taking away deductions claimed for that income) will be taxed at higher rates | | Only have other income (such as a family trust distribution) | your other income (after taking away deductions claimed for that income) will be taxed at higher rates | Table 5: How income of a person under 18 years old is taxed To check the individual tax rates of an adult, see: - [Tax rates – Australian resident](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-australian-residents) - [Tax rates – foreign resident](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/tax-rates-foreign-residents) QC72762 Print or Download
