[[1]] Expense payment fringe benefits | Australian Taxation Office — https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits
    extract (page read): [Skip to main content](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#content) [Skip To search](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#search-box) [Skip To Alex Virtual Assistant](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#alex-virtual-assistant) # Expense payment fringe benefits Check if you provide expense payment fringe benefits to your employees, and calculate the taxable value of the benefits. **Last updated** 11 August 2026 Print or Download ## On this page - [What is an expense payment fringe benefit?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Whatisanexpensepaymentfringebenefit) - [Exempt expense payment benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Exemptexpensepaymentbenefits) - [What to do if you provide an expense payment fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Whattodoifyouprovideanexpensepaymentfringebenefit) - [Taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Taxablevalueofanexpensepaymentfringebenefit) - [Records you need to keep](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Recordsyouneedtokeep) - [Learning resources](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Learningresources) ## What is an expense payment fringe benefit? An expense payment fringe benefit may arise when an employee incurs an expense for their own benefit and you, as their employer either: - reimburse them for the expense - directly pay a third party for the expense. Expense payment fringe benefits only arise from expenses your employee incurs. Goods or services you provide to an employee, or pay for with your credit card, aren't expense payment fringe benefits. In these cases, the goods or services may be [property fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/property-fringe-benefits) or [residual fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/residual-fringe-benefits). An expense payment fringe benefit may be for: - a business or private expense, or a combination of both - an expense incurred by an associate of the employee, such as their partner or relative. ### Common expense payment fringe benefits Common examples of expense payment fringe benefits include, but are not limited to, the reimbursement or payment of: - car expenses, such as registration and insurance - car parking (if you don't provide the car parking facilities) - home mortgage expenses - cost of acquiring a home desktop computer - home telephone and internet expenses - employee personal credit card payments - health insurance premiums - self-education expenses. ### Changes to salary sacrificed work-related expense payment fringe benefits from 1 April 2027 From 1 April 2027, the fringe benefits tax (FBT) treatment of salary sacrificed work-related expense payment fringe benefits covered by the standard deduction will change. #### What's changing? Currently, you can use the [otherwise deductible rule](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/reducing-your-fbt-liability#ato-Providingbenefitsthatwouldbedeductiblefortheemployee) to reduce your FBT liability where your employee could have claimed an income tax deduction for the expense if they paid for it themselves. From 1 April 2027, you'll no longer be to use the otherwise deductible rule to reduce your FBT liability for salary sacrificed work-related expense payment fringe benefits that are covered by the [standard deduction](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/standard-deduction-for-work-related-expenses), regardless of value. #### What isn't changing? The change doesn't apply to: - work-related expense payment fringe benefits provided through a salary sacrifice arrangement that aren't covered by the standard deduction - expense payment fringe benefits provided outside a salary sacrifice arrangement. You can continue to apply the otherwise deductible rule to reduce your FBT liability for work-related expense payment fringe benefits that are covered by the [standard deduction](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/standard-deduction-for-work-related-expenses), if they aren't salary sacrificed. ##### Example: annual self-education expense Bec is a pharmacist who attends an annual one-day conference each year in August to maintain and update her professional knowledge. Bec's annual conference expenses are paid for under a salary sacrifice arrangement with her employer, BeWell Pharmacies Co. Under the arrangement, BeWell Pharmacies Co. pays for the: - return flights costing $300 - taxi travel costing $150 - conference registration costing $250. ###### Before 1 April 2027 Bec attends the conference in August 2026. Her employer can use the otherwise deductible rule to reduce the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit, because Bec could have claimed an income tax deduction for the expense if she paid for it herself. As a result, BeWell Pharmacies Co. may have a reduced or no FBT liability in relation to the conference expenses. Bec cannot claim the expenses as an income tax deduction because she didn't incur the costs herself. **After 1 April 2027** Bec attends the conference in August 2027. Her employer can no longer use the otherwise deductible rule to reduce the FBT liability because: - the benefit is salary sacrificed, and - it’s a work-related expense payment fringe benefit covered by the standard deduction. As a result, the conference expenses will be subject to FBT. BeWell Pharmacies Co. pays FBT on the grossed-up taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefits. As self-education expenses are covered by the standard deduction, Bec cannot claim the expenses as itemised deductions in her personal income tax return. End of example ## Exempt expense payment benefits You don't pay FBT if the expense payment fringe benefit is for an [exempt benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt), such as a: - [minor benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/minor-benefits-exemption), or - [work-related item](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/work-related-items-exempt-from-fbt) that is exempt from FBT, such as portable electronic devices, protective clothing or tools of trade. Exempt benefits differ from [reductions and concessions](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Reductionsandconcessions) you may be able to apply to the taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit. If the benefit is exempt, you don't need to calculate its taxable value. ## What to do if you provide an expense payment fringe benefit You need to: 1. work out the [taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Taxablevalueofexpensepaymentfringebenefi) 2. [calculate how much FBT to pay](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt) 3. [keep the appropriate records](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Recordsyouneedtokeep) 4. [lodge your FBT return](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/lodging-your-fbt-return-and-paying) 5. [pay the FBT amount](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/lodging-your-fbt-return-and-paying) 6. check if you need to [report the fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/reportable-fringe-benefits) through Single Touch Payroll (or on your employee’s payment summary). ## Taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit Generally, the taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit is the amount you reimburse or pay. Find out how to calculate the taxable value of [common expense payment fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00010&PiT=99991231235958/#9.9). ### Reductions and concessions You may be able to reduce the taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit (or eliminate it entirely) if: - the [otherwise deductible rule](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/reducing-your-fbt-liability#ato-Providingbenefitsthatwouldbedeductiblefortheemployee) applies – that is, if your employee could have claimed an income tax deduction for the expense if they had paid for it themselves; you must [keep records](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Recordsyouneedtokeep) to support your claim - your employee incurred the expense to purchase goods or services from your business – these are known as [in-house expense payment fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00010&PiT=99991231235958/#9.3) - the benefit is eligible for an [exemption or concession](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt), such as for relocation expenses or living away from home expenses. ## Records you need to keep For FBT purposes, you must [keep records](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/record-keeping-for-fbt) that: - show how you calculated the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit - support any exemption or concession you used. ### Records and the otherwise deductible rule If you use the otherwise deductible rule, you must have certain documents to demonstrate the extent to which the expense would be deductible to the employee. This is a [substantiation requirement](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV%2FFBTGEMP%2F00010&PiT=99991231235958&anchor=9.5#9.5). This may include: - a travel diary kept by the employee or - an [employee declaration](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/employee-declarations). Or, you can choose to rely on [FBT alternative record keeping](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/record-keeping-for-fbt/fringe-benefits-tax-alternative-record-keeping) for expense payment fringe benefits as detailed in the [LI 2024/6 legislative instrument](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?docid=OPS/LI20246/00001) and [LI 2024/6 explanatory statement](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22ESO%2FESLI20246%22&PiT=99991231235958). ## Learning resources You can access our free [expense payments fringe benefits taxExternal Link](https://smallbusiness.taxsuperandyou.gov.au/expense-payments-fringe-benefits-tax) course on the [Essentials to strengthen your small businessExternal Link](https://smallbusiness.taxsuperandyou.gov.au/) online learning platform. and (b) if the recipient had, at the time when the recipients expenditure was incurred, incurred and paid unreimbursed expenditure (in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) called the [gross expenditure](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s152a.html#gross_expenditure)), in respect of the same matter in respect of which the recipients expenditure was incurred, equal to: (i) in the case of an in \- house expense payment fringe benefit--the amount that, but for this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) and Division 14 and the recipients contribution, would be the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax; or (ii) in the case of an external expense payment fringe benefit--the amount of the recipients expenditure; a once \- only deduction (in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) called the gross deduction ) would, or would if not for Divisions 28 and 900 of the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1997](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/), have been allowable to the recipient under that Act or the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1936](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/)in respect of the [gross expenditure](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s152a.html#gross_expenditure); and (ba) the amount (in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) called the notional deduction ) calculated in accordance with the formula: ![Start formula GD minus RD end formula](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A03280_image.17.png) where: "GD" is the gross deduction; and "RD" is: (i) if there is no recipients portion in relation to the expense payment fringe benefit--nil; or (ii) if there is a recipients portion in relation to the expense payment fringe benefit--the amount (if any) that would, or that would but for Divisions 28 and 900 of the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1997](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/), have been allowable as a once \- only deduction to the recipient under that Act or the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1936](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/)in respect of the recipients expenditure (assuming that any payment of that expenditure by the recipient had been paid by the recipient at the time when the recipients expenditure was incurred); exceeds nil; and (c) in the case of an expense payment fringe benefit that is not an eligible incidental travel expense payment benefit or an eligible overtime meal expense payment benefit: (ia) where the recipients expenditure is in respect of fuel or oil for a motor vehicle owned by, or leased to, the recipient: (A) where the fringe benefit is an eligible small expense payment fringe benefit or an undocumentable expense payment fringe benefit--substitute documentary evidence of the recipients expenditure is maintained by or on behalf of the provider and, if the provider is not the employer, that documentary evidence, or a copy, is given to the employer before the declaration date; or (B) in any case--documentary evidence of the recipients expenditure is obtained by the recipient and that documentary evidence, or a copy, is given to the employer before the declaration date; or (C) in any case--the recipient gives to the employer, before the declaration date, a declaration, in a form approved by the Commissioner, in respect of the recipients expenditure; or (i) where subparagraph (ia) does not apply and the fringe benefit is an undocumentable expense payment fringe benefit or an eligible small expense payment fringe benefit: (A) documentary evidence of the recipients expenditure is obtained by the recipient and that documentary evidence, or a copy, is given to the employer before the declaration date; or (B) substitute documentary evidence of the recipients expenditure is maintained by or on behalf of the provider and, if the provider is not the employer, that documentary evidence, or a copy, is given to the employer before the declaration date; or (ii) in any other case--documentary evidence of the recipients expenditure is obtained by the recipient and that documentary evidence, or a copy, is given to the employer before the declaration date; and (d) where the expense payment fringe benefit is an extended travel expense payment benefit (other than an international aircrew expense payment benefit)--the recipient gives to the employer, before the declaration date, a travel diary in relation to the travel undertaken by the recipient to which the fringe benefit relates; and (e) except where the expense payment fringe benefit is: (i) an exclusive employee expense payment benefit; or (ia) covered by a recurring fringe benefit declaration (see section [152A)](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s152a.html); or (ii) an eligible overtime meal expense payment benefit; or (iii) an eligible incidental travel expense payment benefit; or (iv) an extended travel expense payment benefit; or (v) a [car expense payment benefit](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s53.html#car_expense_payment_benefit); the recipient gives to the employer, before the declaration date, a declaration, in a form approved by the Commissioner, in respect of the recipients expenditure; and (ea) where: (i) the expense payment fringe benefit is a [car expense payment benefit](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s53.html#car_expense_payment_benefit) in respect of a car held by the recipient during a period (in this section called the holding period ) in the year of tax; and (ii) the substantiation rules set out in Division 15 have been complied with in relation to the car in relation to the holding period; the following conditions are satisfied: (iii) the recipient gives to the employer, before the declaration date, a car substantiation declaration for the car for the year of tax; (iv) in a case where the substantiation rules require log book records or odometer records to be maintained by or on behalf of the recipient in relation to the car--the car substantiation declaration is accompanied by a copy of those documents; and (f) if: (i) [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(ea) does not apply; and (ii) the expense payment fringe benefit is a [car expense payment benefit](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s53.html#car_expense_payment_benefit) in respect of a car held by the recipient during a period (the holding period ) in the year of tax; the recipient gives a declaration to the employer, before the declaration date and in a form approved by the Commissioner, that purports to set out: (iii) the holding period; and (iv) the number of whole business kilometres travelled by the car during the holding period; and (v) the number of whole kilometres travelled by the car during the holding period; the taxable value, but for Division 14, of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax is the amount calculated in accordance with the formula: ![Start formula TV minus ND end formula](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A03280_image.18.png) where: "TV" is the amount that, but for this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) and Division 14, would be the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax; and "ND" is: (g) if neither [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(ea) nor [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(f) applies and [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(l) does not apply--the notional deduction; or (h) if [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(ea) applies and [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(l) does not apply--whichever of the following amounts is applicable: (i) if it would be concluded that the amount of the providers portion would have been the same even if the recipients expenditure were not incurred in producing assessable income of the recipient--the business use percentage of the amount that, but for this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) and Division 14, would be the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax; (ii) if subparagraph (i) does not apply: (A) in the case of an in \- house expense payment fringe benefit--the business use percentage of the amount that, but for this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) and Division 14 and the recipients contribution, would be the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax; or (B) in the case of an external expense payment fringe benefit--the business use percentage of the recipients expenditure; or (j) where: (i) [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(f) applies; and (iia) [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(l) does not apply; whichever of the following amounts is the least: (iii) the notional deduction; (iv) if it would be concluded that the amount of the providers portion would have been the same even if the recipients expenditure were not incurred in producing assessable income of the recipient--33â…“% of the amount that, but for this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) and Division 14, would be the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax; (v) if subparagraph (iv) does not apply: (A) in the case of an in \- house expense payment fringe benefit--33â…“% of the amount that but for this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) and Division 14 and the recipients contribution, would be the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit in relation to the year of tax; or (B) in the case of an external expense payment fringe benefit--33â…“% of the recipients expenditure; or (l) if, under [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection)138(3), the expense payment fringe benefit is deemed to have been provided to the recipient only--the amount calculated in accordance with [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection)(9). (1A) [Subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection)(1) does not apply in relation to the recipient of an expense payment fringe benefit in relation to a year of tax if: (a) the benefit is provided to the recipient under a salary packaging arrangement; and (b) the gross deduction would be a kind of deduction mentioned in a ny of [paragraphs](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph) 25 \- 130(2)(c) to (g) of the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1997](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/). (2) For the purposes of the application of this section in relation to a fringe benefit, where the recipient: (a) while undertaking travel referred to in [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(1)(d), engages in an activity in the course of producing assessable income of the recipient; and (b) does not make, as mentioned in the [definition](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#definition) of travel diary in [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection)136(1), an entry relating to the activity, being an entry of the kind referred to in that [definition](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#definition); the activity shall be deemed not to have been engaged in by the recipient in the course of producing assessable income. (9) For the purposes of [paragraph](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#paragraph)(1)(l) (which applies to an expense payment fringe benefit that, under [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection)138(3), is deemed to have been provided to an employee only), the amount is calculated in accordance with the formula: ![Start formula Unadjusted ND times Employee's percentage of interest end formula](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A03280_image.19.png) where: "employee's percentage of interest" : (a) is the percentage of the interest held by the employee, during a period (in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s37.html#subsection) called the holding period ) in the year of tax, in the asset or other thing that: (i) relates to the matter in respect of which the expense payment fringe benefit is provided; and (ii) is applied or used for the purpose of producing assessable income of the employee; and (b) does not include the percentage of the interest held in that asset or other thing by the employee's associate or associates during the holding period. [Reasonable food and drink amounts for employees living away from home (LAFHA) – overseas](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-rates-and-thresholds#ato-ReasonablefoodanddrinkamountsforemployeeslivingawayfromhomeLAFHAoverseas) ## Current FBT rate A fringe benefits tax (FBT) rate of **47%** applies across the 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027 FBT years. The FBT year runs from **1 April** to **31 March**. To work out earlier rates and exemption thresholds, see [Historical rates and thresholds](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-historical-rates-and-thresholds). See detailed guidance in [Fringe benefits tax – a guide for employers](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view.htm?Docid=SAV/FBTGEMP/00001&PiT=99991231235958). ## Taxation determinations Certain rates and thresholds are referenced from the relevant taxation determination. We publish taxation determinations for: - [motor vehicle (other than a car)](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-rates-and-thresholds#MotorvehicleotherthanacarCentsperkilomet) – cents per kilometre rate - [reasonable food and drink amounts](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-rates-and-thresholds#Reasonablefoodanddrinkamountsforemployee) for employees living away from home. All other rates and thresholds are only available on this page. ## Pay by instalments threshold If your FBT liability for the last year was $3,000 or more, you will need to pay 4 quarterly instalments. ## Rate for 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027 | FBT year | FBT rate | | --- | --- | | Ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | 47% | Table 1: FBT rate for years ending 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027 ## Gross-up rates for FBT ### Type 1: higher gross-up rate This rate is used where the benefit provider is **entitled to a goods and services tax (GST) credit** in respect of the provision of a benefit. | FBT year | FBT rate | Type 1 gross-up rate | | --- | --- | --- | | Ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | 47% | 2.0802 | Table 2: FBT Type 1 gross-up rate ### Type 2: lower gross-up rate This rate is used if the benefit provider is **not entitled to claim GST** credits. | FBT year | FBT rate | Type 2 gross-up rate | | --- | --- | --- | | Ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | 47% | 1.8868 | Table 3: FBT Type 2 gross-up rate ## Reportable fringe benefits If you provide certain fringe benefits with a total taxable value of more than $2,000 during the FBT year, you must report: - the grossed-up taxable value of the fringe benefits on the employee's income statement or payment summary - for the corresponding income year. Reportable fringe benefits are grossed-up using the lower gross-up rate. This is regardless of whether the benefits provided are type 1 or type 2. Work out how to [calculate your FBT](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt). So, for example, if an employee receives certain fringe benefits with a total taxable value of $2,000.01 for the FBT year ending 31 March 2026, the reportable fringe benefits amount is $3,773. | Threshold for reporting on income statements or payment summaries | FBT years ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | | --- | --- | | Taxable value | Exceeds $2,000 | | Minimum grossed-up value | $3,773 | Table 4: Reportable fringe benefits thresholds ## Capping of concessional FBT treatment for certain employers The capping thresholds for the FBT exemption and FBT rebate concessions are shown in Table 5 below. | Employer type | FBT concession for the years ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | | --- | --- | | Public benevolent institution (other than public hospitals) and health promotion charities | FBT exemption capped at $30,000.<br>Salary packaged meal entertainment and entertainment facility leasing expense benefits capped at $5,000. | | Public hospitals, not-for-profit hospitals and public ambulance services | FBT exemption capped at $17,000.<br>Salary packaged meal entertainment and entertainment facility leasing expense benefits capped at $5,000. | | Rebatable employers – certain registered charities, non-government and not-for-profit organisations | FBT rebate of 47% capped at $30,000.<br>Salary packaged meal entertainment and entertainment facility leasing expense benefits capped at $5,000. | Table 5: FBT treatment for certain employers ## Record keeping exemption threshold | FBT year ending | Threshold | | --- | --- | | 31 March 2027 | $10,962 | | 31 March 2026 | $10,664 | | 31 March 2025 | $10,334 | | 31 March 2024 | $9,786 | | 31 March 2023 | $9,181 | Table 6: Record keeping exemption threshold Work out [earlier rates and thresholds](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-historical-rates-and-thresholds). ## Car fringe benefits statutory formula rates A flat statutory rate of 20% applies to all car fringe benefits you provide from 1 April 2014, regardless of the distance travelled. Work out your taxable value and FBT payable with the [car calculator](https://www.ato.gov.au/calculators-and-tools/fringe-benefits-tax-car-calculator). The exception is where there is a pre-existing commitment in place, before 7:30pm AEST on 10 May 2011, to provide a car. Where you have a pre-existing commitment in place, the statutory percentages are available in Chapter 7.8 of _Fringe benefits tax – a guide for employers_. Find out more about FBT for employers in [Chapter 7.8 Statutory formula method](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00008&PiT=99991231235958#7.8). ## Deemed depreciation rate – cars The diminishing value depreciation rates are used for car fringe benefits valued under the operating cost method. For cars purchased on or after 10 May 2006, the depreciation rate is 25%. Find out more about FBT for employers in [Chapter 7.9 – Operating cost method](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/https:/www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00008&PiT=99991231235958#7.9). ## Electric vehicle home charging rate Employers with FBT obligations and individuals with work-related car expenses who meet the eligibility requirements can choose to calculate electricity costs when charging electric vehicles at an employee's or individual's home using the methodology outlined in Practical Compliance Guideline [PCG 2024/2](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=COG/PCG20242/NAT/ATO/00001&PiT=99991231235958) _Electrical vehicle home charging rate – calculating electricity costs when a vehicle is charged at an employee's or individual's home_. The PCG provides that a revised EV home charging rate of 5.47 cents per kilometre can be used for the FBT year starting on 1 April 2026. For previous FBT years, the EV home charging rate is 4.20 cents per kilometre. The test is whether there is any entitlement to a GST input tax credit.\n\nType 1 benefits are grossed-up to a tax inclusive value by applying the higher Type 1 FBT gross-up formula.\n\nThe type 2 aggregate fringe benefits amount represents the total taxable values of all other fringe benefits (or excluded fringe benefits) provided to employees, or their associates, that do not fall within the classification of type 1 fringe benefits.\n\nFringe benefits (including excluded fringe benefits) that are either wholly GST-free[[7]](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22TXR%2FTR20012%2FNAT%2FATO%2Ffp7%22&PiT=99991231235958#fp7) or input taxed[[8]](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22TXR%2FTR20012%2FNAT%2FATO%2Ffp8%22&PiT=99991231235958#fp8) cannot be classified as a type 1 benefit and consequently must be a type 2 benefit.\n\nSome fringe benefits may be supplied that do not entitle the provider to GST input tax credits under the GST Act.\n\nSection 149A(1) states that a GST-creditable benefit arises where there is an entitlement to an input tax credit because of Division 111 of the GST Act.\n\nDivision 111 of the GST Act potentially applies where an employee, or his/her associate[[20]](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22TXR%2FTR20012%2FNAT%2FATO%2Ffp20%22&PiT=99991231235958#fp20), incurs an expense. This can involve the employee paying the expense but does not necessarily require the employee to pay the provider prior to reimbursement.\n\n38. However, where an employee incurs an expense as the employer's agent, for example, in purchasing office stationery on the employer's behalf, the acquisition is made by the employer and not the employee. Hence, Division 111 does not apply. Because the acquisition is made by the employer there is no need for Division 111 to treat a payment as if it is consideration for an acquisition.\n\nDivision 111 of the GST Act treats payments to employees in the form of expense payment benefits as consideration for an acquisition made by the employer so that the employer is entitled to an input tax credit as if the employer had acquired the thing directly from a supplier.\n\nThe payment of the expense incurred by the employee can be either by way of reimbursement to the employee or by direct payment to the supplier of the goods or services to the employee." }

correctness.justification: Conclusions are right: taxable value $132 (220 − 88) and Type 1 gross-up 2.0802 for the FBT year ending 31 March 2023, with s 24 stated from the legislation itself. completeness.justification: Every reference point is covered — the (a) workings table, the Type 1 rate and the GST-credit reason for it, and the FBT computation — plus additional qualifications the reference omits (s 24(1)(e) declaration, s 24(1)(c)(ii) documentary evidence, minor-benefits caveat, the 2027 change). faithfulness.justification: Roughly 80-85% of load-bearing claims are anchored at the claim and verified from captured text: taxable-value rule ([[1]]), the s 24 otherwise-deductible rule and its declaration/documentary-evidence conditions ([[2]], full section text captured), the 2.0802/1.8868 and 47% rates ([[3]]), and the Division 111/'any entitlement' points quoted verbatim from TR 2001/2 ([[4]]). Unverified: the s 20 characterisation and the 'ss 5B, 5C and 149A' follow-on (no markers, uncaptured) — minor, low-importance claims; s 24 is paraphrased rather than quoted inline, though its full text appears in the capture.

helpfulness.justification: Strong structure by sub-question, a workings table for (a), step-by-step computations for (b) and (c), and professionally relevant caveats (s 58P assumption, the 1 April 2027 change); but it does not set the governing statutory words out inline and closes with assumptions rather than a concrete next step (e.g. verify the declaration is in the approved form / retain the bill), an element required at levels 3+.

citation_grounding.justification: Citations are densely anchored at the claim and mostly verified: [[2]] supplies the captured primary text of s 24 for the central reduction rule, [[3]] verifies the 2.0802 gross-up and 47% rate for the correct year (acceptable administrative grounding for rates), and [[4]] verifies the Type 1/Division 111 propositions with quoted passages. A small minority rest on unverified or secondary-only grounding — s 20 and ss 5B/5C/149A are named with no marker or capture, and s 23's taxable-value rule is grounded only in the ATO page — so it falls short of level 5's statute-in-view standard.

[Reasonable food and drink amounts for employees living away from home (LAFHA) – overseas](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-rates-and-thresholds#ato-ReasonablefoodanddrinkamountsforemployeeslivingawayfromhomeLAFHAoverseas) ## Current FBT rate A fringe benefits tax (FBT) rate of **47%** applies across the 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027 FBT years. The FBT year runs from **1 April** to **31 March**. To work out earlier rates and exemption thresholds, see [Historical rates and thresholds](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-historical-rates-and-thresholds). See detailed guidance in [Fringe benefits tax – a guide for employers](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view.htm?Docid=SAV/FBTGEMP/00001&PiT=99991231235958). ## Taxation determinations Certain rates and thresholds are referenced from the relevant taxation determination. We publish taxation determinations for: - [motor vehicle (other than a car)](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-rates-and-thresholds#MotorvehicleotherthanacarCentsperkilomet) – cents per kilometre rate - [reasonable food and drink amounts](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-rates-and-thresholds#Reasonablefoodanddrinkamountsforemployee) for employees living away from home. All other rates and thresholds are only available on this page. ## Pay by instalments threshold If your FBT liability for the last year was $3,000 or more, you will need to pay 4 quarterly instalments. ## Rate for 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027 | FBT year | FBT rate | | --- | --- | | Ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | 47% | Table 1: FBT rate for years ending 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027 ## Gross-up rates for FBT ### Type 1: higher gross-up rate This rate is used where the benefit provider is **entitled to a goods and services tax (GST) credit** in respect of the provision of a benefit. | FBT year | FBT rate | Type 1 gross-up rate | | --- | --- | --- | | Ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | 47% | 2.0802 | Table 2: FBT Type 1 gross-up rate ### Type 2: lower gross-up rate This rate is used if the benefit provider is **not entitled to claim GST** credits. | FBT year | FBT rate | Type 2 gross-up rate | | --- | --- | --- | | Ending 31 March 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 | 47% | 1.8868 | Table 3: FBT Type 2 gross-up rate ## Reportable fringe benefits If you provide certain fringe benefits with a total taxable value of more than $2,000 during the FBT year, you must report: - the grossed-up taxable value of the fringe benefits on the employee's income statement or payment summary - for the corresponding income year. Reportable fringe benefits are grossed-up using the lower gross-up rate. This is regardless of whether the benefits provided are type 1 or type 2. Work out how to [calculate your FBT](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt). [What to do if you provide an expense payment fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Whattodoifyouprovideanexpensepaymentfringebenefit) - [Learning resources](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#ato-Learningresources) ## What is an expense payment fringe benefit? An expense payment fringe benefit may arise when an employee incurs an expense for their own benefit and you, as their employer either: - reimburse them for the expense - directly pay a third party for the expense. Expense payment fringe benefits only arise from expenses your employee incurs. Goods or services you provide to an employee, or pay for with your credit card, aren't expense payment fringe benefits. In these cases, the goods or services may be [property fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/property-fringe-benefits) or [residual fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/residual-fringe-benefits). An expense payment fringe benefit may be for: - a business or private expense, or a combination of both - an expense incurred by an associate of the employee, such as their partner or relative. ### Common expense payment fringe benefits Common examples of expense payment fringe benefits include, but are not limited to, the reimbursement or payment of: - car expenses, such as registration and insurance - car parking (if you don't provide the car parking facilities) - home mortgage expenses - cost of acquiring a home desktop computer - home telephone and internet expenses - employee personal credit card payments - health insurance premiums - self-education expenses. ### Changes to salary sacrificed work-related expense payment fringe benefits from 1 April 2027 From 1 April 2027, the fringe benefits tax (FBT) treatment of salary sacrificed work-related expense payment fringe benefits covered by the standard deduction will change. #### What's changing? Currently, you can use the [otherwise deductible rule](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/reducing-your-fbt-liability#ato-Providingbenefitsthatwouldbedeductiblefortheemployee) to reduce your FBT liability where your employee could have claimed an income tax deduction for the expense if they paid for it themselves. From 1 April 2027, you'll no longer be to use the otherwise deductible rule to reduce your FBT liability for salary sacrificed work-related expense payment fringe benefits that are covered by the [standard deduction](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/standard-deduction-for-work-related-expenses), regardless of value. #### What isn't changing? The change doesn't apply to: - work-related expense payment fringe benefits provided through a salary sacrifice arrangement that aren't covered by the standard deduction - expense payment fringe benefits provided outside a salary sacrifice arrangement. You can continue to apply the otherwise deductible rule to reduce your FBT liability for work-related expense payment fringe benefits that are covered by the [standard deduction](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/standard-deduction-for-work-related-expenses), if they aren't salary sacrificed. ##### Example: annual self-education expense Bec is a pharmacist who attends an annual one-day conference each year in August to maintain and update her professional knowledge. Bec's annual conference expenses are paid for under a salary sacrifice arrangement with her employer, BeWell Pharmacies Co. Under the arrangement, BeWell Pharmacies Co. pays for the: - return flights costing $300 - taxi travel costing $150 - conference registration costing $250. ###### Before 1 April 2027 Bec attends the conference in August 2026. Her employer can use the otherwise deductible rule to reduce the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit, because Bec could have claimed an income tax deduction for the expense if she paid for it herself. As a result, BeWell Pharmacies Co. may have a reduced or no FBT liability in relation to the conference expenses. Bec cannot claim the expenses as an income tax deduction because she didn't incur the costs herself. **After 1 April 2027** Bec attends the conference in August 2027. Her employer can no longer use the otherwise deductible rule to reduce the FBT liability because: - the benefit is salary sacrificed, and - it’s a work-related expense payment fringe benefit covered by the standard deduction. As a result, the conference expenses will be subject to FBT. BeWell Pharmacies Co. pays FBT on the grossed-up taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefits. As self-education expenses are covered by the standard deduction, Bec cannot claim the expenses as itemised deductions in her personal income tax return. End of example ## Exempt expense payment benefits You don't pay FBT if the expense payment fringe benefit is for an [exempt benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt), such as a: - [minor benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/minor-benefits-exemption), or - [work-related item](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/work-related-items-exempt-from-fbt) that is exempt from FBT, such as portable electronic devices, protective clothing or tools of trade. Exempt benefits differ from [reductions and concessions](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Reductionsandconcessions) you may be able to apply to the taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit. If the benefit is exempt, you don't need to calculate its taxable value. ## What to do if you provide an expense payment fringe benefit You need to: 1. work out the [taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Taxablevalueofexpensepaymentfringebenefi) 2. [calculate how much FBT to pay](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt) 3. [keep the appropriate records](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Recordsyouneedtokeep) 4. [lodge your FBT return](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/lodging-your-fbt-return-and-paying) 5. [pay the FBT amount](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/lodging-your-fbt-return-and-paying) 6. check if you need to [report the fringe benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/reportable-fringe-benefits) through Single Touch Payroll (or on your employee’s payment summary). ## Taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit Generally, the taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit is the amount you reimburse or pay. Find out how to calculate the taxable value of [common expense payment fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00010&PiT=99991231235958/#9.9). ### Reductions and concessions You may be able to reduce the taxable value of an expense payment fringe benefit (or eliminate it entirely) if: - the [otherwise deductible rule](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/reducing-your-fbt-liability#ato-Providingbenefitsthatwouldbedeductiblefortheemployee) applies – that is, if your employee could have claimed an income tax deduction for the expense if they had paid for it themselves; you must [keep records](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits/expense-payment-fringe-benefits#Recordsyouneedtokeep) to support your claim - your employee incurred the expense to purchase goods or services from your business – these are known as [in-house expense payment fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00010&PiT=99991231235958/#9.3) - the benefit is eligible for an [exemption or concession](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt), such as for relocation expenses or living away from home expenses. ## Records you need to keep For FBT purposes, you must [keep records](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/record-keeping-for-fbt) that: - show how you calculated the taxable value of the expense payment fringe benefit - support any exemption or concession you used. ### Records and the otherwise deductible rule If you use the otherwise deductible rule, you must have certain documents to demonstrate the extent to which the expense would be deductible to the employee. This is a [substantiation requirement](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV%2FFBTGEMP%2F00010&PiT=99991231235958&anchor=9.5#9.5). This may include: - a travel diary kept by the employee or - an [employee declaration](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/employee-declarations). Or, you can choose to rely on [FBT alternative record keeping](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/record-keeping-for-fbt/fringe-benefits-tax-alternative-record-keeping) for expense payment fringe benefits as detailed in the [LI 2024/6 legislative instrument](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?docid=OPS/LI20246/00001) and [LI 2024/6 explanatory statement](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22ESO%2FESLI20246%22&PiT=99991231235958). ## Learning resources You can access our free [expense payments fringe benefits taxExternal Link](https://smallbusiness.taxsuperandyou.gov.au/expense-payments-fringe-benefits-tax) course on the [Essentials to strengthen your small businessExternal Link](https://smallbusiness.taxsuperandyou.gov.au/) online learning platform. Find out how FBT applies, what you need to do as an employer, and what deductions you can claim. **Last updated** 17 July 2024 Print or Download ## On this page - [What is fringe benefits tax?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-Whatisfringebenefitstax) - [What is a fringe benefit?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-Whatisafringebenefit) - [Who receives fringe benefits?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-Whoreceivesfringebenefits) - [Who pays FBT?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-WhopaysFBT) - [How much FBT do you pay?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-HowmuchFBTdoyoupay) - [Can you claim deductions and GST credits?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-CanyouclaimdeductionsandGSTcredits) - [What do you need to do?](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-Whatdoyouneedtodo) - [FBT – a guide for employers](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/how-fringe-benefits-tax-works#ato-FBTaguideforemployers) ## What is fringe benefits tax? Fringe benefits tax (FBT) is a tax paid by employers on certain benefits provided to their employees, or to their employees’ family or other associates. FBT is separate to income tax. It's calculated on the taxable value of the fringe benefit. As an employer, you must self-assess your FBT liability for the FBT year (1 April to 31 March). If you have an FBT liability, you must lodge an FBT return and pay the FBT you owe. ## What is a fringe benefit? A fringe benefit is like a payment to an employee, but in a different form to salary or wages. There are different types of fringe benefits. Examples include: - allowing an employee to use a work car for private purposes - car parking - paying an employee's gym membership - providing entertainment by way of free tickets to concerts - reimbursing an expense incurred by an employee, such as school fees - giving an employee a discounted loan - giving benefits under a salary sacrifice arrangement with an employee. The following are **not** fringe benefits: - salary and wages - employer contributions to complying super funds - shares or rights provided under approved employee share acquisition schemes - employment termination payments (including, for example, the gift or sale at a discount of a company car to an employee on termination) - payments deemed to be dividends under Division 7A - benefits provided to volunteers and contractors - exempt benefits, such as certain benefits provided by religious institutions to their religious practitioners. ## Who receives fringe benefits? FBT applies to fringe benefits provided to your employees, or to your employees' families or other associates. For FBT purposes, an employee includes a: - current, future or past employee - director of a company - beneficiary of a trust who works in the business. If you're a sole trader or a partner in a partnership, you are not an employee. Benefits you provide to yourself are not subject to FBT. Your clients are not employees. Benefits you provide to clients, such as entertainment, are not subject to FBT. ## Who pays FBT? The employer pays FBT. This is the case even if the benefit is provided by a third party under an arrangement with the employer. ## How much FBT do you pay? To work out how much FBT to pay, you 'gross-up' the taxable value of the benefits you've provided. This is equivalent to the gross income your employees would have to earn, at the highest marginal tax rate (including the Medicare levy), to buy the benefits themselves. The FBT you pay is 47% of this 'grossed-up' value of the fringe benefits. ### Example: FBT on a gym membership Jenni runs a small consulting firm. She provides her employee, Anton, with a gym membership that costs $1,100 (including $100 GST). This is a fringe benefit. Jenni works out the FBT as follows: Taxable value of the benefit ($1,100) × the gross-up rate (for a GST-inclusive fringe benefit the rate is 2.0802) × the FBT rate (47%) = FBT of $1,075.46. Jenni must prepare and lodge an annual FBT return, and pay her FBT liability. She may also need to calculate and report Anton's reportable fringe benefits amount in his end-of-year payment information. As the gym membership is subject to FBT, Jenni can claim: - an income tax deduction and GST credit for the cost of the gym membership - an income tax deduction for the FBT paid. End of example ## Can you claim deductions and GST credits? As an employer, you can claim: - an income tax deduction and GST credits for the cost of providing fringe benefits - if you can claim GST credits, you claim the GST-exclusive amount as an income tax deduction - if you can't claim GST credits, you claim the full amount as an income tax deduction - an income tax deduction for the FBT you are required to pay. ## What do you need to do? As an employer, you need to: 1. Identify the [types of fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits) you provide. 2. Check for FBT concessions and ways you can reduce FBT. - Some [benefits are exempt from FBT](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt), such as work-related items. - You can [reduce your FBT liability](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/exemptions-concessions-and-other-ways-to-reduce-fbt/reducing-your-fbt-liability) by using alternatives to fringe benefits or providing benefits that are eligible for a concession. - If you're a not-for-profit employer, you may be eligible for an [exemption or rebate for not-for-profit organisations](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-concessions-for-not-for-profit-organisations). 3. Work out the [taxable value of fringe benefits](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits) you provide. 4. [Calculate your FBT liability](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt). 5. [Keep records, including employee declarations where needed](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/record-keeping-for-fbt). 6. [Lodge an FBT return and pay the FBT you owe](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/lodging-your-fbt-return-and-paying). 7. [Report each employee's fringe benefits in their end-of-year payment information, if required](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/reportable-fringe-benefits). ## FBT – a guide for employers [Fringe benefits tax – a guide for employers](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV/FBTGEMP/00001&PiT=99991231235958) is an additional resource to help you meet your FBT obligations as an employer. It explains: - FBT and your responsibilities as an employer - how to identify and value each type of benefit, and what concessions are available - the meaning of terms used throughout the guide. We link to the guide throughout our web content to provide more comprehensive information on a topic, where required. Authorised by the Australian Government, Canberra. [What you need to do](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt#ato-Whatyouneedtodo) - [How to calculate FBT – business and government](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt#ato-HowtocalculateFBTbusinessandgovernment) - [How to calculate FBT – for FBT-exempt and rebatable not-for-profit organisations](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/calculating-your-fbt#ato-HowtocalculateFBTforFBTexemptandrebatablenotforprofitorganisations) ## What you need to do As an employer, you must self-assess the amount of fringe benefits tax (FBT) you have to pay. To work out how much FBT you have to pay, you 'gross-up' the taxable value of the benefits you've provided. This reflects the gross salary your employees would have to earn, at the highest marginal tax rate (including Medicare levy), to buy the benefits themselves. The FBT you owe is the grossed-up amount multiplied by the FBT rate. You pay this amount to us by the date your FBT return is due, which is generally 21 May. ## How to calculate FBT – business and government Use the steps below if you are a: - business - government organisation - [not-for-profit organisation that is not exempt from FBT and not eligible for the FBT rebate](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-concessions-for-not-for-profit-organisations). ### Step 1: Work out the taxable value of each fringe benefit - How you work out the taxable value of a fringe benefit varies according to the [type of benefit](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/types-of-fringe-benefits). - If the cost of the fringe benefit included GST, include this in the taxable value. - If you provided car fringe benefits, you can use the FBT car calculator to work out the taxable value of those benefits. [FBT car calculator](https://www.ato.gov.au/single-page-applications/calculatorsandtools?anchor=FBTCar&anchor=FBTCar/questions#FBTCar/questions) ### Step 2: Add up fringe benefits from step 1 that included GST - These are fringe benefits for which you can claim a GST credit. - Include both reportable and any non-reportable benefits. ### Step 3: Multiply the step 2 amount by the higher gross-up rate - The higher (type 1) gross-up rate is 2.0802. - You can claim GST credits for these fringe benefits. The higher rate takes this into account. - This rate applies for all FBT years since the FBT year ending 31 March 2019. For gross-up rates in earlier years, see [Fringe benefits tax – historical rates and thresholds](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-historical-rates-and-thresholds). ### Step 4: Add up the fringe benefits from step 1 that did not include GST - These are benefits that were either GST-free or input taxed. - Include both reportable and any non-reportable benefits. ### Step 5: Multiply the step 4 amount by the lower gross-up rate - The lower (type 2) gross-up rate is 1.8868. - This rate applies for all FBT years since the FBT year ending 31 March 2019. For gross-up rates in earlier years, see [Fringe benefits tax – historical rates and thresholds](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-historical-rates-and-thresholds). ### Step 6: Add up the amounts from steps 3 and 5 - This is your total fringe benefits taxable amount. ### Step 7: Multiply the step 6 amount by the FBT rate - The FBT rate is 47%. - This rate applies for all FBT years since the FBT year ending 31 March 2019. For rates in earlier years, see [Fringe benefits tax – historical rates and thresholds](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/fringe-benefits-tax-historical-rates-and-thresholds). - The amount you have worked out is the total FBT amount you have to pay when you [lodge your FBT return](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-registration-lodgment-payment-and-reporting/lodging-your-fbt-return-and-paying). Start of example Example: calculating how much FBT you have to pay MantCo has 2 employees, Marta and Anthony. Using steps 1–7 above, MantCo calculates its FBT liability as follows. 1. MantCo works out the taxable value of the fringe benefits it provided to its employees: - A car fringe benefit for Marta with a taxable value of $7,700, including GST. - A car fringe benefit for Anthony with a taxable value of $6,600, including GST. - School fees for Anthony's daughter with a taxable value of $6,000. The school fees are GST-free. - Restaurant meals for both Marta and Anthony, with a taxable value of $2,200, including GST. Meals are not reportable benefits, so MantCo does not need to allocate the taxable value of the meals to the individual employees. 2. The total taxable value of the fringe benefits that included GST is: $7,700 (car) + $6,600 (car) + $2,200 (meals) = $16,500. 3. MantCo uses the type 1 rate to gross up the fringe benefits that included GST: $16,500 × 2.0802 = $34,323 (rounded to the nearest dollar). 4. The total taxable value of the fringe benefits that did not include GST is: $6,000 (school fees). 5. MantCo uses the type 2 rate to gross up the fringe benefits that did not include GST: $6,000 × 1.8868 = $11,321 (rounded to the nearest dollar). 6. The total fringe benefits taxable amount is: $34,323 + $11,321 = $45,644 7. MantCo uses the FBT rate to calculate the total FBT it must pay: $45,644 × 47% = $21,452.68. End of example ## How to calculate FBT – for FBT-exempt and rebatable not-for-profit organisations There are additional steps in the FBT calculation if you are a [not-for-profit organisation that is exempt from FBT or eligible for the FBT rebate](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/fringe-benefits-tax/fbt-concessions-for-not-for-profit-organisations). This is because the benefits you provide to your employees are exempt or rebatable, up to a capping threshold for each employee. Use the calculator to work out the FBT payable for the fringe benefits you provide to each of your employees. [Not-for-profit FBT calculator](https://www.ato.gov.au/calculators-and-tools/fringe-benefits-tax-not-for-profit-calculator) ### FBT-exempt employers – calculate FBT manually For FBT-exempt employers, fringe benefits you provide to an employee are exempt from FBT, up to a capping threshold. Any fringe benefits in excess of the capping threshold do not qualify for this exemption. To manually calculate your FBT exempt and non-exempt amounts, see [FBT guide: 6.10 Calculating the FBT exemption](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV%2FFBTGEMP%2F00007#6.10). ### Rebatable employers – calculate FBT manually For rebatable employers, you apply a rebate to the grossed-up value of fringe benefits you provide to an employee, up to a capping threshold. Any fringe benefits in excess of the capping threshold do not qualify for the rebate. To manually calculate your FBT amounts and rebate, see [FBT guide: 6.11 Calculating the FBT rebate](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=SAV%2FFBTGEMP%2F00007#6.11). Work out the FBT to pay, including applying the type 1 or type 2 gross-up rate and the FBT rate. SECT 32.20 The main exception--fringe benefits ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 32.20 **The main exception--fringe benefits** Section 32 \- 5 does not stop you deducting a loss or outgoing to the extent that you incur it in respect of providing \* entertainment by way of \\* providing a \\* [fringe benefit](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#fringe_benefit). But this exception does not apply to the extent that the taxable [value](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#value) of the \\* [fringe benefit](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#fringe_benefit) is reduced [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section [63A](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/s63a.html) of the [Fringe Benefits Tax Assessment Act 1986](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/fbtaa1986312/). Note 1: You may be able to deduct losses or outgoings that are [fringe benefits](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#fringe_benefit) [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section [51AEA](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s51aea.html), [51AEB](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s51aeb.html) or [51AEC](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/s51aec.html) of the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1936](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/). If you do, then you cannot deduct them [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section 8 \- 1 (about [general deductions](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#general_deduction)) and so this section is not relevant. Note 2: There are other exceptions for a loss or outgoing you incur in providing a benefit that would be a [fringe benefit](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#fringe_benefit) if it were not an exempt benefit: see items 1.6 and 1.7 of the table in section 32 \- 30\. #### Navigate - SECT 69.5 Non - deductible expenses do not give rise to creditable acquisitions or creditable importations ### A NEW TAX SYSTEM (GOODS AND SERVICES TAX) ACT 1999 - SECT 69.5 **Non - deductible expenses do not give rise to creditable acquisitions or creditable importations** (1) An [acquisition](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#acquisition) is not a \\* [creditable acquisition](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#creditable_acquisition) to the extent that it is a \\* non \- deductible expense. (2) An [importation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#import) is not a \\* [creditable importation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#creditable_importation) to the extent that it is a \\* non \- deductible expense. (3) An [acquisition](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#acquisition) or [importation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#import) is a non \- deductible expense if it is not deductible under Division 8 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) because of one of the following: (a) section 26 \- 5 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Penalties); (b) section 26 \- 30 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Relative's travel expenses); (c) section 26 \- 40 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Maintaining your family); (d) section 26 \- [45](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s45.html) of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Recreational club expenses); (e) section 26 \- 50 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Expenses for a leisure facility); (f) Division 32 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Entertainment expenses); (g) Division 34 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) (Non \- compulsory uniforms); (h) section 51AK of the \\* [ITAA 1936](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1936) (Agreements for the provision of non \- deductible non \- cash [business](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#business) benefits). (3A) An [acquisition](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#acquisition) or [importation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#import) is also a non \- deductible expense to the extent that it is not deductible under Division 8 of the \\* [ITAA 1997](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1997) because of one of the following: (a) section 51AEA of the \\* [ITAA 1936](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1936) (Meal [entertainment](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#entertainment)--election to use the 50/50 split method); (b) section 51AEB of the [ITAA 1936](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1936) (Meal [entertainment](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#entertainment)--election to use the 12 week register method); (c) section 51AEC of the [ITAA 1936](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#itaa_1936) (Entertainment facility--election to use the 50/50 split method). (4) If the [entity](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#entity) making the [acquisition](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#acquisition) or [importation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#import) is an \* [exempt entity](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#exempt_entity), the [acquisition](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#acquisition) or [importation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#import) is a non \- deductible expense if it would have been a non \- deductible expense under [subsection](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s182.10.html#subsection)(3) or (3A) had the [entity](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#entity) not been an [exempt entity](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsasta1999402/s195.1.html#exempt_entity).
